newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: PRESS DIGEST - South Africa - April 10.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - South Africa - April 10.

text.p: These are the leading stories in the South African press on Thursday.
Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

- African Mining Group, the black empowerment consortium which won the race to buy 34.9 percent of JCI from Anglo American Corp in November, and its black partners have ended up with an effective stake of little more than 11 percent after struggling to interest South African financial institutions in the deal.
- Zairean rebels seized the country's second largest city, Lubumbashi, as President Mobutu Sese Seko sought to end the political chaos in Kinshasa by naming a military chief as premier.
- The National Union of Mineworkers has tabled an opening demand of a 25 percent wage increase for about 5,000 members on De Beers mines.
- Fraud and corruption cases amounting to about 40 million rand were being investigated in 12 national and provincial government departments in KwaZulu-Natal.
- The Japanese have been queueing to get a taste of traditional South African boerewors rolls (country-style hot dogs), at the International School's annual fete in Tokyo.

- Spoornet, South Africa's state-owned railway company, was losing more than 500,000 rand a month on its operations in Zaire because of the civil war, according to Friedel Mulke, head of Spoornet's Comazar subsidiary.

- South African Micro Electronic Systems (SAMES), the Pretoria microchip producer, has been returned to state hands for the second time in its brief history after its partner, Austria Mikro Systeme International AG announced it was baling out of the loss-making venture.
- Japanese tea drinkers consumed 500 tonnes of South African rooibos tea last year, with a retail value of about 50 million rand.
- President Nelson Mandela endorsed policing minister Sydney Mufamadi and Commissioner George Fivaz as the best the country has got to combat its crime scourge.
- Former state president F.W. de Klerk dismissed revelations about his involvement in the formation of a counter- revolutionary force, saying he had already told the "truth commission" all.
- Rebels dealt a potentially fatal blow to the 32-year rule of President Mobutu Sese Seko by wresting control of Zaire's economic backbone.
- Rebel leader Laurent Kabila gave Mobutu three days to contact him with a view to negotiating his departure from power.
- AIDS is surging in South Africa, where poor people end up having sex because they have no money to go to the movies or the swimming pool, Health Minister Nkosazana Zuma said.
